Class I
 Uninfected operative wound, no acute inflammation, primary closure, no break in aseptic technique
 Example: routine excision of cyst 
 Infection Risk <2%

Class II
 Minor break in asepsis, elective entry into a mucosal region
 Example: conjunctival biopsy; suture briefly touches non-sterile surface
 Infection Risk <10%

Class III
 Inflammation without purulent drainage, penetrating traumatic wounds < 4 hours, major break in aseptic technique
 Example: excision of ulcerated, inflamed basal cell carcinoma
 Infection Risk ~20%

Class IV
 Purulent inflammation, devitalized or necrotic tissue, penetrating wounds of > 4 hours or with foreign bodies
 Example: excision of purulent hordeolum
 Infection Risk ~40%

both found in retina, work together

detect when object/predator getting closer to you

cards.definition:
world, federal, state, public, and private organizations
ex. World Health Organization (WHO) Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Institute of Health (NIH)

CDC= training for Healthcare Providers on standard precautions

1. Infectious Agent: virus, bacteria, other microbe(s)
2. Reservoir (source): places where infectious agents live (e.g., sinks, surfaces, human skin, hands, lungs)
3. Portal of Exit: mouth (sneeze or cough), cut in skin
4. Mode of Transmission: a way infectious agents are moved to the susceptible person; more to come ex. droplets
5. Portal of Entry: mouth (inhalation, consume), cut in
skin
6. Susceptible Host: person; may be healthy or immunocompromised

break chain at any link to stop spread

Airborne: inhalation, microscopic
ex. influenza, varicella (chickenpox)

Droplet: inhalation, bigger than airborne
ex. Rhinovirus (cold), COVID-19

Contact: person-to-person, handshake, tonometer tip
ex. Norovirus, adenovirus (pink eye)

Bloodborne: exposure to infected blood
ex. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

Vector: living organism that transmits infection to human
ex. Lyme disease (deer ticks)

Oral: water/food
ex. Cholera, hepatitis A (HepA)

1. Recognize and manage the reservoir of the infectious agent
ex. throw away old eye makeup containers

2. Control routes of transmission
ex. hand washing, mask wearing, immunizations

1. Hand hygiene (hand washing)= 20 sec, start of exam, before and after touching patient, use alcohol based in healthcare

6. Respiratory hygiene (cough etiquette)

1 - Zygote travels from fallopian tube to womb and embeds in uterine lining; cells arrange into a ball and begin to form embryo and support system.
2,3- Embryo forms three layers, which will become the nervous system and skin; muscles, bones, and circulatory system; and digestive system, lungs, and glands; neural tube also develops
4- Neural tube continues to develop into the brain and spinal cord; primitive heart is visible, as are leg and arm bud

10-12- Heart develops its basic adult structures; spine and ribs develop more fully; brain forms major divisions

13-24 -Lower body growth accelerates; external genitalia are fully developed; body develops hairy outer covering; fetus can make basic facial expressions; fetal movements can be felt by mother

25-38 -Fetus triples in size; brain and lungs are sufficiently developed at 28 weeks to allow survival outside of womb; visual and auditory systems are functional; fetus is capable of learning and behaviors begin to emerge

• The People of Puerto Rico (1956) marked two major developments in anthropology: 
⎼ First, it represented an anthropological study of a culture already well known to the Western world (unlike the Trobriand Islanders studied by Malinowski) 
⎼ Second, Steward's work was the result of a team effort, rather than that of a solitary anthropologist living within a foreign culture. 
• The People of Puerto Rico was the result of both Steward's time spent on the island as well as that of several of his students.

• In the 1970s and 1980s, anthropology began to learn an important lesson about reflexivity, or critical self-examination. 
• The lesson came when Annette Weiner returned to the Trobriand Islands to study the same culture as Malinowski had. 
• She found that her previous male counterparts had witnessed only part of the culture. 
• This increased reflexivity has aided anthropology to become a more holistic and carefully considered discipline.

• Jean Briggs studied Inuit communities in Canada, focusing on how families trained children to properly manage and express emotions. 
• Her book Never in Anger (1971) used reflexivity to show how the anthropologist herself was subject to training by the family she lived with.

• After the turn to increased reflexivity, anthropologists began investigating their own cultures. 
• Her work demonstrated the power of anthropology to illuminate not only the lives of others, but our own lives as well, what Victor Turner called "being thrice-born"

1) Motor neuron releases acetylcholine into the neuromuscular junction. ach binds to receptors on sarcolemma causes depolarization

3) Ca2+ binds to troponin on actin filament, causing a shift in tropomyosin and exposure of the myosin head binding site 

4) Shortening of the sarcomere occurs, forming a cross-bridge and pulling the actin filament along the thick filament, resulting in contraction.

5) Muscle relaxes when acetylcholine is degraded by acetylcholine esterase and the allowing Ca2+ is brought back into the SR. ATP binds to myosin head, allowing it to relax from actin.

1. Rods and cones contain a cell membrane protein, opsin, that is uniquely sensitive to light
2. When retinal in a rhodopsin (or other opsin) molecule absorbs a photon, the configuration of the protein changes
3. triggers a series of changes that lead to a reduction in cGMP. cGMP regulates the activity of voltage-sensitive Na+ and Ca++ ion channels that keep the photoreceptor depolarized
4. In darkness, levels of cGMP are HIGH, and ion channels stay OPEN allowing cations to flow in (depolarized, resting state)
5. . In the light, cGMP levels DROP and some of the channels CLOSE, leading to HYPERPOLARIZATION, reduces noise and inc sensitivity, different from all other sensory systems that cause depolarization
6. In the dark, when photoreceptors are relatively depolarized and proportion of open ion channels is high, the rate of transmitter release from the photoreceptor is correspondingly HIGH. 
7. In the light, when receptors are hyperpolarized and the number of open ion channels is LOWER, the rate of transmitter release is LOWER. 
8. Transmitter changes from the photoreceptor cause graded potential changes in bipolar cells, which either trigger (or not) action potentials from the ganglion cells.

2. local GRADED potential phase: (EPSP) Positive potential depolarizes the membrane from -60 mV to -40 mV (Threshold phase) 

3. Rapid DEPOLARIZATION Phase: At threshold potential begin rapid Na+ channel opening and rapid influx of Na+ ions (INSIDE GETS MORE POSITIVE WITH RESPECT TO OUTSIDE). (Rising phase) 

4. REPOLARIZATION Phase: Membrane potential moves from positive to negative (+40 to -60 mV), due to closing of Na+ channels, and opening of K+. K+ rushes out. (INSIDE GETS MORE NEGATIVE WITH RESPECT TO OUTSIDE). The potential briefly overshoots in HYPERPOLARIZATION. (Falling phase) 

5. RECOVERY: Sodium-potassium pumps move ions back to correct resting state, which is negative (-60mV).

cards.term: how nervous system works with muscles
cards.definition:
An axon terminal of an efferent neuron makes a synapse called a neuromuscular junction with a muscle fiber. 
action potential arrives at that junction releases acetylcholine, which triggers an action potential in the muscle fiber that moves in all directions over its surface through T tubules. 
action potential reaches the end of the T tubules, ion channels are opened in the sarcoplasmic reticulum that allow Ca ions to flow from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol. 
Troponin then binds the ion and undergoes a conformational change that allows tropomyosin to enter the grooves in the actin helix of the thin filaments. As a result, the myosin-binding sites are uncovered, and the crossbridge cycle is turned on, leading to muscle contraction.

cards.term: Interaction of B cell with helper T cell.

The linkage between cells stimulates the helper T cell to secrete interleukins that activate the B cell and then stimulate the B cell to proliferate, producing a clone of those B cells with identical B-cell receptors
